To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of patients with cancer are not diagnosed with any psychiatric disorder, and that adjustment disorder is the most prevalent diagnosis among cancer patients.
cognitive therapy (CT) is a promising treatment for adjustment disorder in breast cancer patients and that CT may be a useful treatment for adjustment disorder across cancer diagnoses.
Cognitive therapy for adjustment disorder (AD) is effective in reducing the psychological distress of cancer patients and their families, and in reducing the use of psychotropic medication.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the psychological adjustment to a cancer diagnosis, and the psychological adjustment of the patient's family members.
the psychological and social impact of cancer and the development and testing of psychological interventions to help patients and their families to cope better with the impact of cancer.
the development, evaluation, and refinement of cognitive-behavioral interventions for the treatment of adjustment disorder in cancer.

the cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an effective and efficient psychotherapeutic intervention that can help cancer patients to cope with stress, anxiety, and depression and to improve their quality of life.

the evidence for the effectiveness of CBT in cancer patients is limited and inconclusive, but the results of some trials are promising.
